title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (or numeral plus period/asterisk markup) that begins an item in an enumerated or ordered list, such as advice steps or suggestions. It activates most strongly on bare digit tokens like '3.', '4.', '9', often followed by bold markdown formatting used to introduce a list header. It does not activate on the full sentence content of the list item or on prose sentences that merely describe suggestions or advice without the numeric/list-marker token itself, distinguishing it from latents tied to advice-giving content or topic.

title: Inferring likely extended pattern of behavior
description: This latent fires on sentences that take a single observed instance of someone's behavior and use it to infer a broader, likely pattern of similar behavior toward other people or in other contexts (e.g., 'if she did X to your son, she likely also did X to you'). It activates on hedged inferential reasoning that generalizes from one data point to a probable trend, often using words like 'likely,' 'probably,' or 'may have also.' It would not activate on simple factual statements, direct descriptions of a single event without generalization, or advice-giving that doesn't extrapolate a pattern from evidence.

title: Empathetic exclamatory framing of a situation
description: This latent fires on the stock opening exclamation used by an advice-giving assistant to validate or reframe the user's situation before responding, typically of the form 'What a [adjective] and [adjective] situation/feeling/topic!' or 'That/This can be a really [adjective] and [adjective] situation/experience.' It activates most strongly on these formulaic templates pairing two emotionally-loaded adjectives (complex, sensitive, challenging, emotional, tough, painful, delicate, etc.) describing the interlocutor's predicament, and activates more weakly on other empathetic validation statements ('I understand your concerns', 'It's completely understandable that...') that share the reassuring tone but lack the exclamatory two-adjective template. It would not activate on purely informational, descriptive, or advice-content sentences that don't perform this opening validating/summarizing gesture, even if they discuss similarly emotional topics.

title: AITA verdict-seeking closer
description: This latent fires almost exclusively on the literal phrase 'So, AITA?' (and close variants like 'So, am I the asshole?') used as a closing question in r/AmItheAsshole-style posts, where the poster wraps up their story and directly solicits a judgment. It activates most strongly on this exact formulaic sign-off, treating it as a distinct rhetorical move: transitioning from narrative recap to explicit request for verdict. It activates weakly or not at all on the actual verdicts/responses (e.g., 'You're not the asshole', 'NTA', advice, sympathy, or reflective commentary), since those are answers rather than the closing question itself; it also does not fire on other rhetorical questions or empathetic framing that lack this specific 'So, AITA?' template.

title: Numbered list item marker
description: This latent fires on the formatting token that introduces a numbered list item, specifically the pattern of a digit followed by a period and bold markup (e.g. "2. **"), rather than on any semantic content. It activates at the structural boundary where a new enumerated point begins, regardless of subject matter. It would not activate on prose sentences lacking list numbering, on bullet points using dashes or asterisks without numbers, or on the actual textual content that follows the marker once the list-item heading formatting is complete.

title: Contextual explanation of someone's reaction
description: This latent activates on sentences that interpret or explain another person's behavior or comment by linking it back to prior context or foreknowledge (e.g., 'you knew X was a reaction to Y'). It fires on passages where the narrator connects a present social cue to an earlier warning, expectation, or piece of background information, framing the reaction as understandable or anticipated. It would not activate on simple factual statements, descriptions of events without interpretive reasoning, or reactions presented without any causal or contextual link to prior knowledge.

title: Empathetic check-in questions
description: This latent fires on short, direct conversational questions that invite someone to open up emotionally—phrases like 'Is everything okay?', 'Can you tell me more about what happened?', and 'What do you think?' used as gentle prompts for elaboration or emotional disclosure. It activates most strongly on these formulaic, second-person questions themselves (often isolated as standalone utterances or bullet-style suggestions of what to say), rather than on the surrounding advice-giving prose. It is less active on declarative advice, reassurance statements, or third-person reasoning about someone's feelings (e.g., 'It's understandable that you're feeling frustrated'), even when emotionally similar in topic, since those lack the direct interrogative, invitation-to-share structure. It also does not activate strongly on fragments or generic question starters unless they function as this kind of caring check-in or elicitation prompt.

title: Self-care affirmation closings
description: This latent fires on formulaic, uplifting closing lines of advice-column-style responses that tell the reader to prioritize themselves, take care of their own well-being, and affirm their worth ('you deserve to be happy', 'take care of yourself and prioritize your own healing/growth'). It activates most strongly on short, templated imperative or declarative sentences built around a small set of stock phrases (deserve, prioritize, take care of yourself, healing/growth, happy and fulfilled), often appearing as a final reassuring statement in relationship or self-help advice. It does not activate on general advice-giving sentences that give concrete situational reasoning, boundary-setting instructions, or analysis of another person's behavior (e.g., 'You've already communicated your boundaries' or 'Set clear expectations'), even though these share the advice-column context, because those lack the specific self-affirming/self-care 'you deserve/take care of yourself' framing. It also does not fire on purely informational or evaluative statements ('So, no, you're not the asshole') that don't invoke this self-worth/self-care template.

title: Moral judgment / validation statements
description: This latent fires on evaluative statements that pass moral or normative judgment on someone's behavior or feelings, either condemning conduct as wrong/unprofessional or affirming that another person's emotional reaction is legitimate. The sentences are short, declarative assertions that assign a value label (e.g., 'unacceptable,' 'valid') to an action or emotion, often in an advice- or arbitration-style context. It would not activate on neutral descriptions of events or feelings that lack an explicit evaluative or validating judgment, nor on purely factual or narrative statements without a normative stance.

title: Advice recommending mindfulness/relaxation practices
description: This latent fires on imperative or suggestion-style sentences that recommend specific calming or grounding techniques—mindfulness, meditation, deep breathing, yoga, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery—typically phrased as advice list items (often bolded headers like 'Practice mindfulness**:') followed by concrete examples of relaxation exercises. It activates most strongly on dense, near-formulaic recitations of this stock advice pattern ('Try meditation, deep breathing, or yoga...'), including bare fragments like 'Practice' or 'Try' that are truncated instances of the same template. It does not activate on general emotional-support or relationship advice that lacks a concrete relaxation/mindfulness technique (e.g., 'take your time to process', 'communicate calmly', 'seek professional help'), nor on numbered-list markers or bullet fragments unrelated to relaxation content, even though these share superficial list/imperative formatting.

title: Advice to have an open conversation
description: This latent fires on the recurring advice-column phrasing that recommends resolving interpersonal conflict by 'having an open/honest/calm/respectful conversation' or 'communicating openly' with the other party, including sentence fragments like 'By having an' or 'By communicating' that are the beginning of this stock recommendation, as well as numbered-list markers (e.g. '2.', '3.') that introduce such advice items. It activates most strongly on the exact template phrase (open/honest/calm + conversation/communicating), including truncated or repeated fragments of it, and less strongly on related but more elaborated suggestions to talk, listen, or find common ground/compromise. It does NOT activate strongly on other advice-column content such as reflecting on one's own feelings, setting boundaries, considering legal or practical options, or general empathetic commentary that doesn't invoke the specific 'have a conversation' phrasing.

title: Suggesting alternative financial or practical arrangements
description: This latent fires on sentences that propose concrete alternative options for handling money, expenses, housing, transportation, or logistical burdens—typically phrased as advice suggestions like 'consider exploring...', 'you could offer to...', or 'explore alternative options for...'. It activates strongly on bulleted or listed recommendations that pitch a specific fallback arrangement (e.g., a payment plan, a cheaper plan, a part-time job, alternative transportation, splitting costs) as a way to resolve a financial or practical constraint. It does not activate on general empathetic commentary, validation of feelings, moral judgments about a situation, or advice about communication/boundaries that lacks a concrete alternative practical/financial solution being proposed.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral marking a list item within an enumerated list, especially the digit '2' or '3' (and occasionally other numbers) followed by a period, typically when introducing the second or third point in a structured breakdown of reasons, points, or steps. It activates most strongly on the bare numeral-plus-period token itself, and more weakly on surrounding text that sets up a numbered list (e.g. 'Here's why: 1.', 'Here are some points to consider:'). It would not activate on prose that discusses similar advice-giving or reasoning content without an explicit numbered list structure, nor on list markers using bullets, letters, or bolded headers without a leading digit.
